splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on which circuit they are in.

positions.label: Conjunctive ('and' means 'and')
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: Disjunctive ('and' means 'or')
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions that carry criminal consequences.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency interpretations in the criminal context. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit panel held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has taken on new significance after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity must be applied before deferring to an agency's anti-defendant interpretation of an ambiguous criminal provision.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference can override the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous criminal provisions to stand.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses such as conspiracy, or whether Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses like conspiracy to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation of the guideline or an impermissible expansion. This affects whether prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career-offender predicates. The Sentencing Commission has since amended the guideline text, but the split affects many pending and past cases.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is valid
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline entitled to deference under Stinson and Kisor.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is invalid
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled, or whether any state-scheduled substance suffices. The Eighth Circuit has held there is no requirement to match federal schedules, while other circuits have required such a match. This affects base offense levels and career-offender determinations for many defendants.

positions.label: No federal-schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled.

positions.label: Federal-schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's amendments to § 924(c) stacking) can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in the law can support compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit in Crandall and the Seventh Circuit in Thacker held that non-retroactive changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, even in combination with other factors. Other circuits have permitted courts to consider such changes. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to allow this, but the Seventh Circuit held the Commission exceeded its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, particularly in combination with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a Bureau of Prisons decision regarding the conditions or execution of confinement (such as denial of earned time credits or prerelease custody) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions about the execution of their sentences (such as First Step Act time credits), or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) are also available. The Eighth Circuit has acknowledged this unresolved conflict persisting for over half a century, affecting how prisoners seek judicial review of BOP decisions.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for fact/duration challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy, following Preiser v. Rodriguez strictly.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge certain BOP decisions through civil rights actions even when the challenge touches on duration of confinement, particularly when the primary challenge is to conditions or procedures.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether property appreciation occurring between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that post-petition appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor. This split directly affects debtors' ability to retain home equity gains when converting bankruptcy chapters.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of § 541(a), means post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under the Bankruptcy Code's structure and the purpose of § 348(f), post-petition, pre-conversion property appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to promoting reentry and public safety.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at what dissenters describe as 'the extreme of a circuit split.' Other circuits have held that the purpose of supervised release revocation sentencing is not punishment but rather facilitating reentry into the community and protecting the public.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for their violations of supervised release conditions when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punishment is not permissible
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should focus on the defendant's breach of trust and community reentry, not on punishing the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is governed by the civil 30-day deadline or the criminal 14-day deadline.
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to a 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledged the split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a).

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, subject to the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that measurement date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date, providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of the most current and accurate data available.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, based on the equitable principle that a fugitive should not benefit from flight.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that courts lack authority to toll supervised release without explicit statutory authorization, and that the supervised release term runs regardless of whether the supervisee absconds.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously raised — when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any previously presented claim; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, adding an additional gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, and such prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements for successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. Some circuits have recognized candidate standing based on competitive injury, while others have required more particularized showings of harm. The resolution affects the ability to challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices.

positions.label: Candidate standing recognized
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law changes the rules governing how votes are counted.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate standing denied or limited
positions.summary: Holds that candidates must show more than generalized competitive injury to establish standing, particularly for pre-election challenges to voting procedures.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The circuits appear divided on whether orders denying motions to seal medical records qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held that the strong privacy interest in medical information constitutes a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have taken a more restrictive approach to the collateral order doctrine for sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical information are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the interest can be adequately vindicated through other means such as protective orders.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: In re City of New York

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards applicable to discrimination claims arising in hospitality and service industry contexts, including questions about liability and remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently contested.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Adopts broader standards for establishing discrimination liability in hospitality or service establishments, with more expansive remedies available.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, limiting the scope of liability and available damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
